content: The recommendations provided are not intended to evaluate the appropriateness of specific examinations or tests in contexts other than contraceptive use. For instance, while some tests may not be necessary for the safe and effective use of contraception, they could still be relevant for preventive healthcare or for diagnosing and assessing suspected medical conditions. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) concluded that the benefits of these recommendations outweigh any potential harms, classifying them as strong recommendations. For repeat injections of subcutaneous depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA-SC), the GDG determined that the recommendations align with those for intramuscular DMPA (DMPA-IM). These recommendations include guidance on the standard reinjection interval, management of early or late presentations for reinjection, switching between types of progestogen-only injectables (POIs), and handling cases where the previous type of POI or timing of injection is unknown. It is recommended to administer repeat DMPA-SC injections every three months. Guidance is also available for early and late injections. The quality of evidence supporting these recommendations is categorized as very low, but the strength of the recommendation remains strong. A systematic review identified evidence on the timing of reinjection for DMPA and norethisterone enanthate (NET-EN) to ensure continued contraceptive efficacy. This review included studies from PubMed up to November 2008, with an updated search through January 2014. Among 327 citations retrieved, no additional articles met the inclusion criteria. Of the 20 studies included in the systematic review, 10 examined DMPA use, and two specifically referenced DMPA-SC. These studies reported the time to first ovulation following a single DMPA injection, with one comparing the return of ovulation between DMPA-SC and DMPA-IM users. The earliest individual rise in serum progesterone indicating ovulation occurred on day 70 (week 10) for DMPA-IM users, but further evaluation did not confirm ovulation. For DMPA-SC users, the earliest rise occurred on day 106 (week 15). Another study followed 24 women who received a single DMPA-SC injection and found ovulation suppression in 23 women for at least 112 days (16 weeks). The GDG based its recommendations for repeat DMPA-SC injections on evidence from both DMPA-IM and DMPA-SC, as the two formulations are therapeutically equivalent. Despite the very low quality of direct evidence, the GDG considered the benefits of preventing unintended pregnancies and the barriers to safe and consistent contraceptive use. Women's values and preferences, including factors such as choice, ease of use, side effects, and efficacy, were integral to the recommendation process. The GDG emphasized facilitating access to contraceptive methods while maintaining safety and efficacy. The GDG also reviewed evidence on the combined contraceptive transdermal patch and vaginal ring (CVR) for inclusion in the Selected Practice Recommendations (SPR). When direct evidence for these methods was unavailable, the GDG extrapolated from evidence on combined oral contraceptives (COCs). Recommendations for initiating the patch and CVR are consistent with those for COCs. Women can start the patch or CVR within five days of menstrual bleeding onset or at any other time if reasonably certain they are not pregnant. Additional guidance is provided for scenarios such as amenorrhea, postpartum, post-abortion, and switching from other contraceptive methods. The quality of evidence for the patch is moderate to low, while no direct evidence exists for the CVR. The strength of the recommendation is strong. A systematic review identified 18 studies on CHC initiation, including COCs, the patch, and the CVR, on different days of the menstrual cycle. No differences in pregnancy rates were observed based on starting schemes. Side effects, including bleeding patterns, did not vary based on initiation day. The Quick Start method was associated with higher initial continuation rates, but differences in continuation did not persist over time. The GDG concluded that evidence on COCs could be extrapolated to the patch and CVR due to similarities in safety profiles and hormone types/doses. The GDG considered barriers to safe and consistent contraceptive use and the benefits of preventing unintended pregnancies. Women's values and preferences were central to the recommendations, which aim to balance access, safety, and efficacy. The GDG also reviewed the examinations and tests needed before initiating the patch and CVR. Recommendations align with those for COCs and address breast exams, pelvic/genital exams, cervical cancer screening, routine lab tests, hemoglobin tests, STI risk assessment, STI/HIV screening, and blood pressure screening. Blood pressure measurement is desirable before initiation.
